name: Paradox of tolerance
scope: The paradox of tolerance as Karl Popper put it in note 4 to chapter 7 of The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945): unlimited tolerance of the intolerant lets the intolerant destroy tolerance, so a tolerant society may claim the right not to tolerate intolerance (by force only if its opponents refuse rational argument; suppression of their speech is unwise while argument and public opinion can contain them), and may treat incitement to intolerance and persecution as criminal. The scholarship (Stanford and Internet Encyclopedias of Philosophy, Mounk, the FEE essay) also treats the wider debate over whether and when a tolerant society may restrict the intolerant, with Rawls's answer in A Theory of Justice (tolerate the intolerant, except when the tolerant sincerely and with reason believe their own security and the institutions of liberty are in danger) as the main rival formulation. Excluded: general liberal toleration (Locke, Mill) and Marcuse's 'repressive tolerance', which the sources reviewed do not tie to the paradox.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Popper's note says incitement to intolerance and persecution should be treated as criminal, like incitement to murder, which supports legal limits on hateful speech. The same note says suppressing the utterance of intolerant philosophies is most unwise while rational argument and public opinion can keep them in check, and Mounk and the FEE essay read it as no warrant for hate-speech laws. Both are Popper's words, so the sources point both ways.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The paradox allows suppressing only movements that refuse rational argument and answer with fists or pistols; for intolerant philosophies that can be countered by argument, Popper calls suppression most unwise. Suppressing political opposition as such contradicts that.

summary: The paradox of tolerance holds that a society which tolerates everything, the intolerant included, will see tolerance destroyed. Popper concluded that a tolerant society may claim the right not to tolerate intolerance, using force only when opponents refuse rational argument, and may punish incitement to intolerance. Rawls and others reply that the intolerant should be tolerated unless they endanger the security of free institutions.
